L01.note: Only option with neither a stray comma nor a fragment-making participle.

L02.note: 2x2 grid; nearest noun 'eggs' is plural so the trap is 'stay', key is singular head + singular verb.

L03.note: 'but also' completes an implied 'not only' and 'books ... offer' is the only internally agreeing correlative option.

L05.note: Dangling-modifier set: the only option whose subject is a person (the ornithologist).

L06.note: Comma options split subject from verb; nearest word 'sends' is singular so the trap is 'casts', key 'cast'.

L07.note: Progressive and bare -ing look like distractors; singular vs plural is a coin flip.

L08.note: Dangling-modifier set: the only option that puts the agents (the new owners) directly as subject in a plain active clause.

L09.note: 'but also' completes 'not only'; infinitive parallels an implied 'to' phrase.

L10.note: Subject of 'concluded' takes nominative 'I'; the 'report and mine' variants are distractor rewrites.

L11.note: Comma after subject (A) and no punctuation (D) look wrong; semicolon vs comma is a coin flip.

L13.note: Only option with consistent objective case after the preposition ('him ... whom').

L15.note: Classic 'most of them' comma-splice trap; 'most of whom' is the standard key shape.

L16.note: Only correctly punctuated absolute phrase; C is an independent clause (splice), B lacks the comma, D breaks the absolute.

L17.note: 'whoever' as subject of its own clause, and 'but to' parallels an implied 'not to'.

L18.note: Likely 'one of the rivers ... is' trap, but singular vs plural is not decidable from the set.

L19.note: Trailing comma implies a comma-opened nonessential clause; the dash options are unbalanced.

L21.note: 'not that ... but that' vs 'not because ... but because' cannot be told apart; number is a coin flip.

L22.note: Closing dash implies a dash-opened appositive; singular verb is the residual guess.

L23.note: Comma options split subject from verb; only unpunctuated finite option.

L24.note: Uniquely balanced comma pair around the appositive.

L27.note: Only option with subject-verb agreement and no comma between subject and verb.

L28.note: Comma options split subject from verb; nearest noun 'plain' is singular so the trap is 'suggests', key 'suggest'.

L29.note: Object case 'me' plus the closing comma of a nonessential phrase.

L30.note: Conditional-perfect shape looks most key-like; no real signal.

L31.note: Colon is the usual key among punctuation variants; no real signal.

L32.note: 'together with' does not pluralize, so singular 'remains' with the comma pair is the only internally consistent option.

L33.note: Series with internal commas: semicolons between items, comma inside the appositive.

L34.note: 'whoever' as subject of the following clause; A adds a redundant 'that'.

L35.note: Comma after the introductory 'October' eliminates B; whether a nonessential follows is undecidable.

L36.note: 'lime, that' is out; restrictive 'that' vs nonrestrictive 'which' is a coin flip.

L37.note: Subject of 'had' takes 'whoever'; the -ing variants are fragments.

L39.note: Dangling-modifier set: the only option with Dr. Halloran as the subject.

L40.note: Restrictive 'those that' is the only clean contrast form; B is a fragment after a semicolon, A dangles.

L41.note: Agreement plus sense: the engineer, not the design, 'was able to span'.

L42.note: Comma options split subject from verb; nearest noun 'bones' is plural so the trap is 'outlast', key 'outlasts'.

L43.note: Comma options split subject from verb; nearest noun 'council' is singular so the trap is 'identifies', key 'identify'.

L44.note: Uniquely balanced comma pair around the appositive.
